title: What Nikole Hannah-Jones Doesn’t Say
author: Charles C. W. Cooke
summary: Charles C. W. Cooke refuses to join the praise for Nikole Hannah-Jones's mea culpa, calling her original school choice morally indefensible and analytically ignorant. His central target is her 2024 claim that her daughter is not worth more than any other child, which he calls an ugly sentiment that contradicts a parent's natural and proper duty to prioritize their own children. He argues that her experiment was incoherent on its own terms, since the school she chose was no less segregated and she failed at the close parental involvement she claimed would make it work. Cooke's sharpest complaint is that the essay never says what she now believes or what American schools should look like, which he says reduces it to a humblebrag. He closes with a personal attack on a career he sees as rewarded without real mastery.
points: Cooke argues a parent's job is to prioritize their own children without apology, and that only totalitarian ideology has historically broken that instinct.
Hannah-Jones's husband raised the right objection in 2016 when he asked whether they were experimenting on their child.
He notes that her chosen school enrolled more students of her daughter's race, undercutting the stated aim of avoiding segregation.
The essay's omission of what she now believes about education policy is, for Cooke, what keeps it from being brave.
quotes: For penning this mea culpa, Hannah-Jones has received a good deal of praise. Well, you can count me out of all that. Her actions were morally indefensible and analytically ignorant, and her supposed metamorphosis remains invisible to the naked eye.
My job as a parent is to prioritize my children. I owe it to them, and they rely upon me to follow through with that obligation.
Some readers have responded to Hannah-Jones’s admission by proposing that the fault lay not in her instinct, but in its execution.
Yet, by her own admission, she was so neglectful of her daughter’s progress that, for years, she remained unaware that she had fallen badly behind.
What does Hannah-Jones believe now? She doesn’t say. By itself, this omission prevents her essay from being “brave” or “admirable” and relegates it to the status of a humblebrag.

Given that she has extremely strong views about what, how, and where other American children should be taught, it would be useful to know what, having watched her assumptions fail her own child, she now thinks America’s education system should look like.
